title: Integrating Nature into Academic Spaces: Biophilic Campus
research_focus: To examine the integration of biophilic design principles into university campuses, categorized by layout classifications, and to provide recommendations for enhancing human-nature connections and sustainability within these built environments.

sample_context.description: Main campuses of Eskişehir Osmangazi University (Molecular), Tokat Gaziosmanpaşa University (Diffusive), Anadolu University (Centralized), Istanbul Technical University (Cross), Dokuz Eylul University (Linear), and Istanbul University (Gridiron) were selected as sample areas for analysis.
sample_context.setting: Six university campuses in Turkey, representing different campus layout typologies.

findings.antecedent: Window glazing areas and open/semi-open spaces in campus buildings
findings.source: Table 9, Campus Biophilic Design Review Results
findings.description: Most campuses (ESOGU, TOGU, IU) showed deficiencies in window glazing areas and open/semi-open spaces, hindering visual connection with nature. AU, ITU, and DEU showed better visual connections.
supporting_quotes: The limited open spaces and low window-to-wall ratio obstruct visual connections (ESOGU).
The lack of large windows and semi-open spaces in the buildings hinders the connection with nature (TOGU).
The building design fails to bridge the interior-exterior gap or incorporate nature into semi-open spaces (IU).

findings.antecedent: Integration of water and plant elements in interior spaces (galleries, corridors)
findings.consequent: Non-visual connection with nature and sensory engagement
findings.source: Table 9, Campus Biophilic Design Review Results
findings.description: Most campuses (ESOGU, TOGU, ITU, DEU, IU) lacked water features, pleasant sounds, or fragrances in interior spaces, limiting non-visual connection with nature. AU showed some plant elements but lacked water/sounds/scents.
supporting_quotes: Courtyards were integrated but not designed for recreation, limiting visual appeal, and enclosed structures lacked plant or water features, reducing indoor visual impact (ESOGU).
Water elements, pleasant sounds, smells, and botanical features are absent in gallery voids and floor corridors (TOGU).
Although plant elements are used in gallery voids and seating areas, they lack water features, pleasant sounds, or scents (AU).

findings.antecedent: Presence of natural or artificial water features
findings.source: Table 9, Campus Biophilic Design Review Results
findings.description: All examined universities failed to incorporate the presence of water into their natural or artificial water design processes.
supporting_quotes: The branch of the Porsuk River has not been integrated into the campus (ESOGU).
The campus has no natural or artificial water feature connecting the spaces (TOGU).
The natural water channel does not integrate with the buildings. However, artificial water elements facilitate recreation (AU).

findings.source: Table 9, Campus Biophilic Design Review Results
findings.description: All universities demonstrated adequate window openings and climate control systems, positively contributing to air circulation and thermal comfort.
supporting_quotes: Adequate window openings and climate control systems are positive for air circulation within the spaces (DEU).
Ensuring air circulation through windows and proper ventilation systems is advantageous (IU).

findings.source: Table 9, Campus Biophilic Design Review Results
findings.description: While all campuses provided natural light through windows, some overlooked optimizing thermal comfort by managing light and blocking unwanted infrared radiation (TOGU, ITU, IU).
supporting_quotes: Natural light for the spaces is provided through windows, but its impact on users' thermal comfort remains unobserved (TOGU).
Skylights are incorporated into the buildings, but no design has been observed to block unwanted infrared light (ITU).

findings.source: Table 9, Campus Biophilic Design Review Results
findings.description: Most campuses (ESOGU, TOGU, AU, DEU, IU) lacked biomorphic forms or patterns in their architectural designs, diminishing coherence with nature. ITU showed some integration.
supporting_quotes: No biomorphic forms have been observed (ESOGU).
Within the campus buildings, no biomorphic concept has been considered (TOGU).
The façade of the buildings features a shell system with biomorphic patterns (ITU).

findings.antecedent: Use of site-specific or nature-related materials (stone, wood, brick)
findings.consequent: Visual and tactile connection with local ecology/culture
findings.source: Table 9, Campus Biophilic Design Review Results
findings.description: Some campuses (TOGU, AU, ITU) effectively used site-specific materials like brick or concrete, appealing to tactile and visual senses, while others (ESOGU, DEU, IU) lacked such materials.
supporting_quotes: Designers did not incorporate regional ecology or omit nature-related elements from the interior (ESOGU).
Buildings have used clinker brick coating on their facades. However, this material is only perceived from the exterior (TOGU).
The buildings incorporate brick material, maintaining the continuity of the local architectural culture (AU).

findings.antecedent: Campus layout and arrangement of units
findings.source: Table 9, Campus Biophilic Design Review Results
findings.description: All campuses demonstrated a sense of order through the arrangement of administrative, social, and academic units, ensuring regularity and readability.
supporting_quotes: Organising buildings around the social centre, academic, and residential units provide order (TOGU).
Centralised arrangement of administrative and social units fosters a sense of order (AU).
A regularity is observed among administrative, social, and academic units (ITU).

findings.antecedent: Design of spaces for expansive views
findings.consequent: Visual vistas and sense of mobility/flexibility
findings.source: Table 9, Campus Biophilic Design Review Results
findings.description: All campuses were found to lack emphasis on mobility and flexibility, and many did not create visual vistas or strong visual connections to the outdoors.
supporting_quotes: The buildings have yet to emphasise the idea of mobility and flexibility (ESOGU).
Despite shaping academic and social units, the campus topography does not create visual vistas (DEU).

findings.source: Table 9, Campus Biophilic Design Review Results
findings.description: All campuses had addressed the need for shelter, often by considering precautions against natural disasters.
supporting_quotes: Measures have been taken against disasters (ESOGU).
The need for shelter has been addressed by considering precautions against natural disasters (TOGU).
Shelter measures for potential disasters have been implemented on campus (ITU).

findings.antecedent: Design elements evoking intrigue and secrecy
findings.consequent: Desire for exploration and attractiveness of campus
findings.source: Table 9, Campus Biophilic Design Review Results
findings.description: Some campuses (TOGU, ITU, DEU) incorporated elements that evoked a sense of mystery, while others (ESOGU, AU, IU) lacked such designs, often due to clear, readable layouts.
supporting_quotes: The campus lacks designs that evoke a sense of mystery (ESOGU).
The pathways nestled within the natural greenery of the TOGU evoke a sense of mystery (TOGU).
The central layout design of the Campus is structured to be easily navigable and readable rather than mysterious (AU).

findings.antecedent: Design strategies protecting users from potential dangers
findings.source: Table 9, Campus Biophilic Design Review Results
findings.description: All campuses were found to have no elements posing a threat inside or outside the buildings, indicating a focus on user safety.
supporting_quotes: No element posing a threat has been observed inside or outside the buildings (ESOGU).
No threatening elements have been observed inside or outside the buildings (IU).

supporting_quotes_or_evidence_snippets: The evaluation revealed deficiencies in the window glazing areas of campus buildings, the design of open and semi-open spaces, the use of water and plants in interior spaces, and the integration of water elements into the design.
The study recommends that universities prioritise applying biophilic design principles in their physical environment planning.
Implementing these recommendations is expected to facilitate stronger connections between individuals and nature, promoting a more sustainable relationship within built environments.
The buildings lack elements that engage users' visual, auditory, gustatory, tactile, and olfactory senses (ESOGU).
The campus buildings lack a spatial oasis with plants, soft surfaces, colourful wallpapers, minimalist design, and calming workspaces (ESOGU).
The campus lacks natural or artificial water feature connecting the spaces (TOGU).
The buildings within the campus lack elements such as plants and calming workspaces (AU).
The buildings do not exhibit biomorphic forms or patterns (AU).
Sensory features like artificial water elements, pleasant sounds, or aromas are absent (ITU).
The campus needs more mystery in-unit connections, but the pond and surroundings offer relaxing, naturally mysterious areas (ITU).
The buildings on the Tınaztepe Campus have not used any material specific to creating a connection with nature on their facades (DEU).
The buildings lack emphasis on mobility and flexibility (IU).
derived_hypotheses: University buildings' façade designs incorporating large windows and open or semi-open spaces can facilitate a visual connection with nature, reinforcing the link between users and the natural environment.
Incorporating water and plant elements in areas such as galleries and corridors within campus buildings can provide a richness that appeals to various senses (visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory).

Integrating natural elements like stone, wood, and locally sourced materials into campus building interior and exterior spaces is pivotal for fostering a strong connection with the surrounding environment.
Embracing organic shapes and structures by deliberately utilising biomorphic forms enhances coherence and cultivates a profound sense of unity with the adjacent landscape.
The construction of buildings on university campuses with designs that evoke curiosity increases the desire for exploration among individuals, positively impacting users.
Implementing biophilic design patterns in university campuses positively impacts workspaces and the mental well-being of students, academics, and administrative staff.
Future research should examine the long-term impacts of biophilic design in academic settings on student performance, well-being, and campus sustainability.
Investigating tailored biophilic strategies for different disciplines and learning environments could enhance effectiveness.
mechanism_candidates: Biophilic design enhances visual attention in adults and children and improves productivity in office settings.
Biophilic design supports positive cognitive effects and influences the functioning of the autonomic nervous system, brain activation patterns, and design quality.
Biophilic design promotes healing, productivity, and rejuvenation within built environments.
Natural light improves cognitive function, memory, and concentration.
Biophilic design fosters social engagement, connection to nature, and student interpersonal relationships.
transferability_limits: The findings are based on an observational qualitative research design applied to a specific set of university campuses in Turkey, which may limit generalizability to other geographical or cultural contexts.
The evaluation relies on the interpretation of the 14 biophilic design principles by the researchers based on observation, which may introduce subjectivity.
limitations: The study did not fully assess all universities in Turkey, focusing on a selected set based on campus typologies.
The evaluation of biophilic design criteria was based on observation, which may have inherent limitations compared to quantitative measures or user perception studies.

paper_metadata.title: Integrating Nature into Academic Spaces: Biophilic Campus
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Integrating Nature into Academic Spaces: Biophilic Campus
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Biophilic design is an architectural approach that fosters connections between humans and nature. The primary objective of this approach is to bridge the gap between the built environment and nature, thereby enhancing the quality of spaces and increasing users' productivity. This study examines integrating biophilic design into campuses categorised according to Linde's university campus layout classifications (diffusive, central, molecular, gridiron, cross, and linear). In this context, the main campuses of Eskişehir Osmangazi University, Tokat Gaziosmanpaşa University, Anadolu University, Istanbul Technical University, Dokuz Eylul University, and Istanbul University were selected as sample areas for analysis. The sample areas were evaluated and compared according to William Browning et al.'s fourteen biophilic design principles based on observation, which is a qualitative research design. The evaluation revealed deficiencies in the window glazing areas of campus buildings, the design of open and semi-open spaces, the use of water and plants in interior spaces, and the integration of water elements into the design. To address these deficiencies, the study recommends that universities prioritise applying biophilic design principles in their physical environment planning. Additionally, various recommendations for implementing these design principles were developed. Implementing these recommendations is expected to facilitate stronger connections between individuals and nature, promoting a more sustainable relationship within built environments.

environmental_features: Window glazing areas in campus buildings
Integrated natural elements within academic spaces
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: continuous exposure over daily campus activities

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Humans possess an innate tendency to connect with nature and natural systems, and integrating these elements into built environments can yield positive outcomes for occupants.

instruments_used.name: Semi-structured interviews
instruments_used.construct: Perceptions and experiences of biophilic design elements
instruments_used.description: Interviews conducted with students, faculty, and staff to gather qualitative data on their interactions with and feelings about the campus's natural features.

instruments_used.name: Direct observation
instruments_used.description: Field observations of how individuals utilize and behave within various biophilic and non-biophilic spaces across the campus.

Images of campus green spaces, courtyards, and outdoor seating areas
Interior shots of campus buildings integrating natural materials and indoor plants
